extracted.intended_audience: research funders, scientometricians, policy makers, and researchers studying peer review and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_short: validating grant peer review with impact measures
extracted.subtask_description: A literature review of studies that test the predictive (external) validity of grant peer review decisions by comparing ex-ante applicant/proposal indicators and ex-post research outputs across a variety of impact metrics. Focus is on which impact measures have been used, their strengths/limitations, and methodological issues for using them to validate review decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliometric measures (publications and citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count- and citation-based bibliometrics: number of publications, journal impact of publication venues, raw and normalized citation counts, h-index and m-index, proportion of papers in top 10% cited, citations/papers per dollar spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most studies use bibliometrics as the primary output metric (69% in the surveyed literature). Bibliometrics require normalization for time and field; multiple normalization methods exist (h-index, m-index, RCR, percentiles) and each has strengths/weaknesses. Citations are influenced by co-author counts, journal prestige, positive-result bias and rhetorical utility; they may not reflect long-term or societal impact. Use with caution and preferably in combination with other indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-ante applicant performance (prior productivity and citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use applicants' prior publication and citation records (ex-ante performance) as objective indicators of input quality to compare against review evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons of funded vs unfunded applicants' prior performance can test whether reviewers select applicants with superior prior records. Many studies show funded applicants outperform unfunded ones ex-ante, but differences are often small and may reflect inherent productivity rather than the quality of peer review. Prior performance is also a strong predictor of future citation performance (confounder/Matthew effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-post project productivity and impact (funded vs unfunded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare outcomes of funded projects to unfunded projects (productivity, citations, patents, etc.) to assess whether funding decisions predicted subsequent impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct external validity test but is methodologically challenging because funding itself may cause increased productivity (confounding). Availability of unfunded controls is limited; results vary across studies. Time window for measuring ex-post impact and disentangling funding effects are critical design considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unfunded controls in validation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of unfunded applicants/projects as a control group when assessing ex-post outcomes of funded projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies with unfunded controls are better able to separate predictive validity of review decisions from the causal effect of funding. The literature shows higher rates of predictive validity in studies that include unfunded controls (e.g., 91% with unfunded controls provided some evidence vs. 71% without), but sample selection and comparability must be carefully managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization of outputs by funding amount (per-dollar metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute outputs (publications, citations, patents) on a per-dollar or per-cost basis (e.g., citations per dollar, papers per dollar) to account for investment size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies find no correlation between review scores and output when normalized by budget, while others find moderate correlation for unnormalized data. Normalizing can reveal diminishing returns and differential efficiency, but choice to normalize should reflect program goals and assumptions about scale effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I and Type II error rates in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Type I error: proportion of funded projects that yield no publications or have lower-than-expected outcomes; Type II error: proportion of unfunded projects that would have been productive (false negatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type I/II error rates are measurable outcomes for validity testing (e.g., observed ~33% unproductive funded grants in one dataset). Estimating Type II errors is harder due to scarcity of follow-up data on unfunded ideas. Error rates depend on funding success rates and on the metric used to define success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altmetrics/social media attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative metrics capturing online attention and engagement: tweet counts, social media posts, article views/downloads, pageviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altmetrics capture attention and non-traditional outputs (blogs, policy white papers, negative results) that bibliometrics miss. They are dynamic and immediate but not yet fully validated and may represent popularity rather than scientific value. Few studies have directly linked altmetrics to funding decisions to date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration metrics (co-authorship, international collaboration, interdisciplinarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of team collaboration shown in proposals and realized in outputs: number/extent of co-authors, international co-authorship, interdisciplinarity indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration can indicate creativity, innovation, and translatability and may be an explicit program goal. Some evidence shows funded applicants have higher ex-post international collaboration; however, interdisciplinarity may be penalized in peer review and show lower funding success despite possible high impact. Choose collaboration metrics aligned with program objectives and interpret in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-funding review of outcomes (post-project peer review and administrative review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct ex-post peer review panels or administrative reviews of funded projects to assess quality, completeness, relevance and whether stated goals were achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-funding peer review can capture contextual qualitative factors not represented in bibliometrics and may show predictive validity, but it is resource-intensive. Post-publication peer review platforms (PubPeer, F1000) can provide crowd-sourced evaluations but have issues with engagement and anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and technology/commercialization outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use patent counts, patent citations, licenses, CRADAs, spin-off companies, product launches, or manager assessments of commercial success as indicators of translational/commercial impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent-based indicators can reflect applied impact but are rare for many grants and attribution is difficult (multiple inputs produce patents). Some studies find small positive associations between review scores and patent output; others find mixed or null effects. Broader mapping approaches (not just direct citation links) may better capture influence on patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and dataset impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ex-post sharing of research data, downloads of datasets, and citations/uses of shared data as measures of impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data sharing can facilitate reproducibility and generate additional uses of data (associated with higher citations in some studies). Incentives are limited and few studies have examined ex-post data sharing relative to funding decisions. Metrics include data downloads, reuse citations, and data repository deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career outcomes and tracking (future funding, positions, satisfaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure later career indicators of PIs: subsequent grant funding (e.g., NIH awards), tenure-track positions attained, career satisfaction surveys, numbers of theses produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career outcomes can reflect long-term benefits of early-career funding. However, they are often influenced by the funding itself, resubmission behavior, and ex-ante differences; studies must control for prior qualifications to isolate predictive validity of review decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple indicators / panel of metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine diverse quantitative and qualitative indicators (bibliometric, patents, collaborations, career outcomes, societal benefits) to form a pluralistic assessment of research impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Leiden manifesto and other best-practice guidance recommend multiple indicators to provide robustness and to account for socio-economic context. Integration requires deciding weights and balancing comprehensiveness with feasibility; frameworks like Payback illustrate comprehensive approaches but are resource-intensive and may suit program- or portfolio-level assessment rather than single projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and normalization of citation metrics (metric selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection among specific citation-based measures (e.g., h-index, m-index, RCR, percentiles) and approaches to normalize for field, time and other confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different normalization approaches can materially change conclusions; each method has trade-offs. Analysts should justify metric choice, apply field/time normalization, and be aware of index-specific biases (e.g., h-index favors senior researchers). Sensitivity analyses across metrics are advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of impact measures with program goals and research context
rubrics_metrics.description: Select indicators that reflect the explicit goals of the funding program (e.g., translational impact, capacity-building, interdisciplinarity) and interpret metrics in qualitative context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact measures should be chosen and weighted according to program objectives; a metric appropriate for one program may be irrelevant for another. Qualitative contextualization (e.g., end-user evaluation) is important for correct interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility, translatability and publication bias as evaluation dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess outputs for indicators of reproducibility, translational progress (bench-to-bedside), and susceptibility to publication bias or inflated results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation-based impact can favor provocative or invalid results; measures of trustworthiness (replication attempts, methodological transparency, PPPR flags) and translatability should be considered when validation aims to capture societal/clinical benefits rather than citation popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to variability and discriminatory power of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that peer review may coarsely discriminate poor from good proposals but has limited ability to finely discriminate among top-tier proposals; variability in project outputs is high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings often show modest correlations and substantial variability; correlations may disappear when low-scoring proposals are removed. Validation studies should account for restricted ranges near funding cutoffs and consider power/sensitivity to detect differences among high-quality proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of high-risk or novel proposals in review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that reviewers may penalize novelty or high-risk proposals, which affects predictive validity for breakthrough outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence suggests penalization of novel, risky proposals; because breakthrough discoveries are rare and often serendipitous, standard bibliometric validation may miss the value of funding high-risk research. Design evaluations to capture long-tailed breakthrough events and not only average outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and crowd-sourced commentary as quality signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PPPR (e.g., PubPeer, F1000) commentary and ratings as indicators of publication trustworthiness and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPPR can augment bibliometrics by providing qualitative critiques, but engagement levels vary and anonymity issues may limit uptake. Where available, PPPR signals can inform assessments of robustness and reliability of outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative indicators of project completion and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Track administrative outcomes such as project initiation, completion, whether stated goals were achieved, dissemination via non-traditional pathways, and timelines to outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These indicators provide essential context to publication- or citation-based measures. For example, funding may increase initiation rates but not completion or publication timing; ignoring administrative outcomes can misclassify successes/failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comprehensive frameworks (e.g., Payback, translational benefits models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply established, multi-domain frameworks that capture knowledge creation, benefits to future research, political/health/economic impacts, latency and attribution over long time horizons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frameworks like Payback aim to capture broad societal value and attribution over decades; they are thorough but labor-intensive and may be more appropriate for program- or portfolio-level assessment than individual-project validation. Trade-offs between depth and feasibility must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution, latency and multiple-input measurement issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the fact that outputs typically arise from many inputs over long time periods, making attribution to a single grant difficult; account for latency of impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal attribution is challenging—thousands of papers may underlie one therapeutic. Validation studies should use mapping approaches, long time windows, and careful causal inference methods to avoid over-claiming attribution to a single funding decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining quantitative metrics with qualitative/end-user evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate quantitative indicators with qualitative assessments from peers, stakeholders, and end-users to capture public/societal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic evaluation that includes stakeholder/end-user perspectives can better capture societal impact beyond bibliometrics. Methods must be chosen and documented; this approach increases validity but requires more resources and explicit criteria for integrating different evidence types.
